Sixty to seventy per cent of men in their sixties have benign prostatic hyperplasia, and 37% of adult men experience erectile dysfunction.

intro:
The prostate, explained in three minutes

The prostate is a male organ about the size of a chestnut. It sits just below the bladder and wraps around the urethra — the passage urine travels through — like a doughnut.

In youth it is about the size of a walnut, and it grows gradually with age. The problem is its position. As the prostate enlarges, the urinary passage running through it is compressed. Rather like lightly squeezing a hose by hand, urine no longer flows freely.

That is why problems of the prostate usually show themselves first as urinary problems. The stream weakens, the urge comes often, and you wake at night to go to the bathroom. They are easy changes to dismiss as "just getting older".

Benign prostatic hyperplasia begins gradually from the forties, is present in 60–70% of men in their sixties, and in almost all men over seventy. It is closer to an ageing change than to a disease. There is nothing whatever to be embarrassed about.

Three things do, however, need to be told apart

NameIn one lineUsual signs
Benign prostatic hyperplasiaAn enlarged prostate compressing the urinary passageWeak stream, frequent urge, waking at night
ProstatitisInflammation or pain in or around the prostatePain in the perineum or lower abdomen, discomfort on passing urine
Prostate cancerA malignant tumour of the prostateUsually no symptoms in the early stages

All three can begin with "difficulty passing urine", but their treatment is entirely different. Telling them apart by examination is therefore the first step.

A one-minute self-check

See whether any of the following applies to you

Passing urine

  • the stream is thinner than it used to be
  • it takes time before the flow starts
  • the flow stops partway through
  • you do not feel empty afterwards
  • the urge returns within two hours / it is hard to hold once it comes
  • you wake once or more at night to pass urine

Pain and men's health

  • the perineum or lower abdomen has felt heavy or painful for three months or more
  • there is pain on ejaculation
  • it is difficult to obtain or maintain an erection sufficient for a satisfying sex life
  • it is hard to control the timing of ejaculation, and this distresses you

Signs that need immediate medical attention

  • there is blood in the urine
  • urine suddenly will not come at all
  • you have a fever with severe pain in the lower back or perineum
ResultWhat to do
1–2 urinary itemsKeep an eye on it, but if you are over 50, have a prostate examination this year
3 or more urinary itemsWe recommend a consultation. An International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) of 8 or above is the point at which treatment is considered
Any pain itemProstatitis needs to be distinguished. Treatment differs completely depending on whether it is bacterial
Any "immediate attention" itemPlease do not delay — come in straight away
None apply + over 50We still recommend an examination, because early prostate cancer has no symptoms

tags.d:
What exactly is it?

It is a state in which the prostate has enlarged and compresses the urinary passage running through it. The prostate itself is not the problem; the discomfort comes from the compression. Age and male hormones are understood to be the main factors.

Does it turn into cancer?

No. Benign prostatic hyperplasia is benign — a change that is not cancer. The two can, however, be present at the same time, and the symptoms are similar, so we check for both.

Treatment comes in stages
StageWhat it involvesPoints to be aware of
1. Watchful waitingIf symptoms are mild, review once or twice a year without treatment. Adjusting when you drink, cutting back on coffee and alcoholThis is not "doing nothing" — it is watching to a plan
2. MedicationAlpha blockers (relaxing the muscle of the urinary passage), androgen inhibitors (reducing prostate size) and othersAlpha blockers can cause dizziness on standing; hormone inhibitors can reduce libido
3. SurgeryEndoscopic prostatectomy (the current standard), laser vaporisation, prostatic urethral lift and othersLaser is reported to involve relatively less bleeding, and the lift procedure a faster recovery
Please tell us when you take cold medicine

Antihistamines, commonly found in cold remedies, can cause acute urinary retention, in which urine will not come at all. At other clinics and pharmacies too, always say "I have benign prostatic hyperplasia".

What you can start doing today
  • do not hold urine for long periods
  • do not drink much after 7 p.m. (this reduces waking at night)
  • cut down on alcohol, coffee and tea
  • keep to a healthy weight — reduce fatty and high-cholesterol food

Why has the antibiotic not worked?

Because prostatitis is not one illness but four different ones. Some are caused by bacteria and some have nothing to do with bacteria. Where it is not bacterial, antibiotics do not work. Examination to identify which type it is therefore accounts for half of the treatment.

The four types
TypeIn plain termsTreatment
Acute bacterialSudden bacterial infection, with systemic symptoms such as chills and achingAntibiotics, antipyretics and analgesics, plenty of rest
Chronic bacterialRecurrent bacterial infectionA long course of antibiotics, anti-inflammatories alongside, changes to daily habits
Chronic non-bacterial
(chronic pelvic pain syndrome)		The most common type. Pain persists without any clear bacteriaDepending on the subtype: alpha blockers, muscle relaxants, physiotherapy — antibiotics are not recommended for the non-inflammatory subtype
AsymptomaticInflammation found incidentally during other testsUsually no treatment is needed
Examination

We take a symptom history, perform a digital rectal examination, carry out the three-glass urine test to locate where bacteria are coming from, and perform ultrasound.

※ Chronic prostatitis is often approached as something to "manage" rather than "cure". Avoiding long periods of sitting, warm baths, regular exercise and managing stress genuinely help.

Prostate cancer has become one of the most common cancers in Korean men. It has two particular characteristics.

  • First, it has almost no symptoms early on. It is not an illness that brings you to the clinic in pain.
  • Second, it is not part of the national cancer screening programme. That programme covers six cancers — stomach, liver, lung, colorectal, breast and cervical — and prostate cancer is not included.

In other words, it is a cancer nobody will tell you about if you simply wait. From the age of 50, you need to arrange the examination yourself.

Who should be more careful

The most important factors are age and family history. Risk is higher if a father or brother has had prostate cancer. If you have a family history, discuss whether to begin screening earlier.

How it is diagnosed — four stages
  1. Blood test (PSA)If the level is above the threshold, we move on to further checks.
  2. Digital rectal examinationIf a hard nodule is felt, we proceed to biopsy regardless of the PSA level.
  3. Ultrasound and MRIWe confirm the size of the prostate and the location of any lesion.
  4. BiopsyTissue is taken with a needle and examined. Definitive diagnosis is made at this stage.
A high PSA does not always mean cancer

PSA also rises with benign prostatic hyperplasia and with prostatitis. We therefore do not judge on a single number, but look at examination, imaging and, where needed, biopsy together. Do not be alarmed by a high figure — simply work through the checks in order.

Prevention and daily habits
  • reduce animal fat; a low-fat, high-fibre diet
  • plenty of fruit and vegetables — tomatoes (lycopene) and green tea are recommended as protective foods
  • regular exercise and a healthy weight

A "prostate examination" is not a single test. It is a process of assessing how much discomfort there is by questionnaire, examining by hand, measuring a blood marker and looking with ultrasound. Through this combination we distinguish benign prostatic hyperplasia from prostatitis and from prostate cancer.

How the day runs
  1. Consultation and questionnaireWe review symptoms and history and complete the IPSS questionnaire.
  2. Basic testsUrine test, blood test (PSA) and digital rectal examination.
  3. Function and imagingUroflowmetry, residual urine measurement and prostate ultrasound.
  4. Explaining the resultsWe look at the results together and decide the next step.
Prostate care by age group
AgeRecommendation
40sExamination if there are symptoms. Otherwise focus on daily habits
50sAnnual PSA and digital rectal examination even without symptoms — early prostate cancer has no symptoms and is not in the national programme
60sAnnual prostate check plus tracking of urinary symptom scores
70s and aboveAnnual check, and review of medicines being taken (including cold remedies)
Those with a family historyDiscuss an earlier starting point with your doctor

※ PSA testing helps with early detection, but it is also a test discussed alongside the possibility of "overdiagnosis" — finding cancers that would never have needed treatment. We explain both the benefit and the limitation and decide with you.

I am considering surgery — what should I check first?

The first step is to establish objectively whether it really is small. International guidelines recommend distinguishing the following three situations at the consultation stage.

  • Genuinely small (micropenis) — where the measurement criteria are met
  • Appearing small because it is buried in fat — obscured by lower abdominal fat. Here weight loss is recommended first
  • Within the normal range but perceived as small — in this case psychiatric assessment and psychological counselling are needed before surgery
What you must be told at the consultation
  • Sensation may change, or pain may persist.
  • The penis may curve or change shape, and erectile dysfunction can occur.
  • Partial results are common, and further procedures may be needed.

International guidelines regard a safe technique and realistic expectations as essential conditions for a good outcome. We explain exactly how far the evidence has been established for each method, and decide together on the option that suits your condition.

※ Enlargement using silicone, paraffin or oil-based fillers is a method international guidelines strongly recommend against. We do not perform procedures of this kind.

Where does premature ejaculation begin?

The international criteria look at three things together.

  • Time — ejaculation almost always before or shortly after penetration, or markedly shorter than before
  • Control — almost never able to delay ejaculation
  • Distress — it causes distress, or leads to avoiding sexual relations

Premature ejaculation is considered present when all three are there. A short time alone does not mean treatment is needed.

Why does it happen?
  • Where it has always been the case — understood to involve a combination of neurotransmitter systems and genetic factors. It is not a matter of willpower or personality.
  • Where it developed later — erectile dysfunction, prostatitis, thyroid problems, lack of sleep and anxiety can all be causes. Treating the cause often improves it.
Treatment — not starting with surgery

Treatment for premature ejaculation does not begin with surgery. International guidelines recommend behavioural therapy and medication first. Topical anaesthetics, medication taken as needed, medication taken daily, and combination therapy where erectile dysfunction is also present — the options are ample.

Among surgical approaches, there are techniques for which the evidence is not established, or which international guidelines do not recommend. We tell you that plainly, and work through the options starting with those best supported by evidence.

Is it just me?

Not at all. About 37% of adult Korean men experience erectile dysfunction: 63% of men in their fifties and 74% of those in their sixties.

Can I put it down to age?

You should not. An erection occurs only when blood vessels and nerves work together. Erectile dysfunction is therefore, not infrequently, the first signal sent by vascular disease such as diabetes, high blood pressure or high cholesterol. A consultation about erectile dysfunction is not only about sexual function — it is an occasion to check the health of your blood vessels overall.

Treatment climbs like a staircase
StepWhat it involvesPoints to be aware of
Step 1
Daily habits		Exercise, weight control, stopping smoking and reducing alcohol, managing chronic conditions, sleep and stressExercise and weight control alone are reported to reduce risk substantially
Step 2
Oral medication		PDE5 inhibitorsThe first-line treatment in international guidelines. Side effects such as headache can occur
Step 2
Injection		A vasodilator injected directly into the corpus cavernosumPain and priapism are possible, so we explain before proceeding
Step 3Vacuum device, penile implantSatisfaction with implants is high, but infection and mechanical failure are possible, and natural erectile function does not return
Regenerative treatment — where it stands today

Regenerative medicine is the fastest-moving research field in urology. We tell you plainly, however, how far it has actually been established.

Low-intensity extracorporeal shockwave therapy has accumulated enough evidence to be offered, alone or alongside existing medication, in mild to moderate erectile dysfunction. PRP injection and stem cell injection, by contrast, are judged by the most recent international guidelines as something that should still be carried out "within the framework of a clinical trial".

We therefore try the well-evidenced treatments thoroughly first. Regenerative approaches come after that, decided together once the expectations and the limits have been explained precisely.

outro:
How we practise urology here

  1. A full historyWe establish when symptoms began and how much discomfort there is, as a score.
  2. Tests to identify the causeWe distinguish hyperplasia from inflammation from cancer by examination.
  3. Looking at the results togetherWe go through the figures and images on screen with you.
  4. Choosing in order of evidenceWe propose the best-evidenced treatments first, and set out their limits at the same time.
A place where hard things can be said easily

Urology is seen as a difficult department to walk into, because urinary and sexual matters are not easy to raise. But these are not rare problems — most men have them. What we value most is an environment in which what is said in the consulting room stays there, and a consultation in which test results are explained exactly as they are.

Frequently asked questions

Is the digital rectal examination very painful?
It can be uncomfortable, but it is usually over in about ten seconds. It is the quickest and most accurate way to assess size, firmness and any nodule. Even with a normal PSA, a nodule felt at this examination leads on to biopsy.
My PSA came back high. Is it cancer?
More likely not. PSA also rises with benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatitis. We therefore do not judge on one number, but work through examination, ultrasound and, if needed, MRI and biopsy in order.
Does benign prostatic hyperplasia need surgery to resolve?
Mostly not. If symptoms are mild we watch; if moderate we control them with medication. Surgery is considered when medication does not control the symptoms or complications develop.
I wake two or three times a night. Will drinking less fix it?
Reducing fluids after 7 p.m. genuinely helps. However, nocturia also arises from bladder problems, heart or kidney problems and sleep disorders, not only from prostatic hyperplasia. It is better to identify the cause and manage it.
I have taken prostatitis medication for a long time without improvement.
Prostatitis has four types, and antibiotics are not recommended for the most common one (chronic non-bacterial). Re-establishing the type comes first.
Is prostate cancer screening part of the national programme?
It is not. The national cancer screening programme covers six cancers: stomach, liver, lung, colorectal, breast and cervical. Prostate cancer is something you have to arrange yourself.
If I take erectile dysfunction medication, will I become dependent on it?
PDE5 inhibitors are the first-line treatment in international guidelines and are not drugs of dependence. If anything, managing the underlying vascular health and daily habits alongside can reduce the need for medication.
Can surgery solve premature ejaculation?
International guidelines do not recommend surgery first. The standard is to try behavioural therapy and medication thoroughly beforehand.
Can stem cells improve male sexual function?
This is still at the research stage. The most recent international guidelines state that stem cell injection should be offered only "after first- and second-line treatment has failed, and within the framework of a clinical trial". We try the well-evidenced treatments thoroughly first, and decide together on anything beyond that only after the limits have been explained precisely.
From what age should I have prostate checks?
We recommend annual PSA testing and digital rectal examination from the age of 50, even without symptoms. If a family member has had prostate cancer, discuss with your doctor whether to begin earlier.
